finding.claim: authorize() is async but is not awaited in DELETE /reports/:id. The 403 rejection never stops the handler, so any authenticated user can delete any report regardless of grants. The unhandled rejection can also crash the process on modern Node.
finding.source: Any authenticated user sending DELETE /reports/<id> for a report they have no 'delete' grant on

trace.note: report is loaded from the attacker-supplied req.params.id
authorize(...) is called without await, so the returned promise is dropped
authorize is async; a missing grant throws inside the promise and only rejects it
db.reports.remove runs immediately, before or regardless of the authorization result

finding.guards_checked: The only guard is authorize(), and its result is ignored here. The PUT route awaits it correctly at line 27. There is no other middleware or ownership check. The global middleware at lines 4-7 only copies the session user.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 throws on a missing grant, but the DELETE handler calls it without await at server.js:20, so the rejection is dropped. The global middleware at server.js:4-7 only copies the session user. The PUT route awaits it correctly at server.js:27.
verdict.reason: server.js:20 calls async authorize() as a bare statement without await, so the 403 throw at server.js:14 only rejects an ignored promise and server.js:21 db.reports.remove still runs for any authenticated user; the PUT route awaits it correctly at server.js:27.

verdict_facts.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 throws 403 on a missing grant, but the call at line 20 is neither awaited nor caught, so it does not block the handler. The middleware at lines 4-7 only copies the session user.
verdict_facts.reason: server.js:20 calls the async authorize() without await, so its 403 rejection (lines 11-14) cannot stop db.reports.remove at line 21, and any authenticated user can delete any report; the PUT route correctly awaits at line 27.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id passes the whole request body to db.reports.update without an allow-list. A user with only 'write' grant can overwrite protected fields such as owner, id or ACL fields, which is mass assignment. This depends on how db.reports.update treats unknown fields, so it is plausible rather than confirmed.
finding.source: JSON body of PUT /reports/:id from a user holding the 'write' grant

trace.note: authorize checks only the 'write' action on the report
The raw req.body is passed straight to the update

finding.guards_checked: No schema validation or field allow-list was found. The authorize check is coarse and does not cover field-level changes. The db implementation is not in the repo, so field filtering inside it could not be checked.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 throws a 403 when the 'write' grant is missing, and the PUT handler awaits it at server.js:27. It only checks the action, not which fields are changed. No allow-list or schema validation exists in the repo.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: server.js:3 parses the body, :27 awaits authorize for 'write', and :28 passes raw req.body to db.reports.update. The attacker needs only an authenticated user with a 'write' grant, and no field allow-list exists in server.js. Whether owner/id/ACL fields can be overwritten depends on db.reports.update, which is not in the repo, so mass assignment can't be confirmed or refuted.

verdict_facts.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 is awaited at line 27 and throws a 403, so it does gate the route on 'write'. There is no field allow-list or schema validation in this file.
verdict_facts.reason: server.js:28 passes raw req.body to db.reports.update after only a 'write' grant check at line 27, but db is not in this directory, so whether it filters protected fields such as owner or ACL cannot be determined.
